keywords.term: Architecture Architecture Analysis and Design Language

div.p: With the wide application of safety critical embedded systems in various fields, some modern software engineering technology must be developed to increase the security of embedded system to insure the safety of people. Based on the Model-Driven Architecture method, this paper deeply research the semantics of AADL (Architecture Analysis and Design Language) models, and design a tool named UCaS, which is integrated in OSATE (Open Source AADL Tool Environment), and can acquire information from AADL code for the schedulability analysis. Finally, this paper shows the efficiency of the UCaS and point out the direction of future work.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: As performance-critical real-time systems are getting more complex, the verification of functional and nonfunctional properties of these systems is becoming even more complex. For example, mission-critical applications are often very complex and at the same time need a rigorous analysis and verification of its non-functional properties, also called quality attributes. Non-functional properties of interest for these systems are, amongst others, timeliness, performance, and safety properties. Verification of these properties is often delayed until testing phase, resulting in a slow and expensive development process, or, in the worst case, failed projects. Verification of nonfunctional properties in early design phases of the development process is therefore more important than ever.

AADL [1] is a textual and graphical language used to model and analyze the software and hardware architecture of embedded systems. These are systems whose operation strongly depends on meeting non-functional system requirements such as reliability, availability, timing, responsiveness, throughput, safety, and security. AADL is used to describe the structure of such systems as an assembly of software components mapped onto an execution platform. It can be used to describe functional interfaces to components (such as data inputs and outputs) and performance-critical aspects of components (such as timing). AADL can also be used to describe how components interact, such as how data inputs and outputs are connected or how application software components are allocated to execution platform components. The language can also be used to describe the dynamic behavior of the runtime architecture by providing support to model operational modes and mode transitions. The language is designed to be extensible to accommodate analysis of the runtime architectures that the core language does not completely support. Extensions can take the form of new properties and analysis specific notations that can be associated with components.

The Open Source AADL Tool Environment (OSATE) supports the development of architecture models for embedded real-time systems based on the AADL standard. OSATE was developed by the Software Engineering Institute of Carnegie-Mellon University as a set of plug-ins on top of the open source Eclipse platform. It was constructed using the Eclipse Modeling Framework (EMF) and the ANTLR parser generator. The set of plug-ins provides a toolset for front-end processing of AADL models. AADL models can be maintained as textual AADL files or as XML-based AADL model files. All works done in this paper are developed in this environment.

div.head: II. SCHEDULING SIMULATION BASED ON AADL
div.p: The Furness [5] Toolset was developed by Fremont Associates, LLC, and researchers at the University of Pennsylvania with support from licensed users and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. It can be used for schedulability analysis about AADL models which contain only periodic threads.

Times [2][3][4] is a modelling and schedulability analysis tool for embedded real-time systems, developed at Uppsala University in 2001. It is appropriate for systems that can be described as a set of preemptive or non-preemptive tasks which are triggered periodically or sporadically by time or external events. It provides a graphical interface for editing and simulation, and an engine for schedulability analysis. But it is not developed for AADL models specially. To know the details of the comparion please refer to [6]。 This paper gives a tool of scheduling and simulation for AADL models which combines the advantages of Furness and Times, which named UCaS. UCaS is a plug-in of OSATE, it can be used to analyze the schedulability of a given System described in AADL. There is a system event producer in this tool, which used to set the trigger time of aperidic threads and sporadic threads.

Figure 1 shows the structure of UCaS. First, necessary information is collected from AAXL file, which is a XML file based on AADL code. And then users can use the event producer to set trigger period and trigger point for aperiodic and sporadic threads. Scheduler gets all these information and analyzes the schedulability of the system, gets a conclusion and gives out the execution trace in the simulator. So, users will know whether the system is schedulable and which thread make the system not schedulable, they can change their design.

div.head: A. System information collector
div.p: When a system model is builded up by user through AADL code, AAXL file, the XML pattern of AADL code, will be generated by OSATE automatically. AAXL file is only an abstract description of system components, it needs to be translated into a specific system instance and used for the next step of schedulability analysis. OSATE provides this function to instantiate AAXL file. UCaS extracted the needed information from AAXL, including the number of processors, scheduling strategy, threads information, the period, deadline, minimum and maximum execution time, the device which the threads bind to, and so on. All these information are stored in a text file by UCaS, and can be used for reading and analyzing by the scheduler.

div.head: B. System event producer
div.p: There are three types of common threads: Periodic thread, aperiodic thread and sporadic thread. They are differed in the dispatch strategies and the response to external events. The period of periodic thread is also its deadline, whenever its period arrives, it will be dispatched and enter the ready queue.

Aperiodic threads can be trigged at any time, there is no time constraint for it. When an instance of aperiodic thread is running, there may be another same instance be trigged, the new instance will join in the dispatching queue and waiting for dispatch, when the instance is completed, the new instance can join in the ready queue and to be scheduled.

There is a period property for the sporadic thread as the periodic thread. The interval of consequent instances of sporadic threads being trigged should not be less than this value. Otherwise, the system would think that it is too often for the trigged threads, there are three ways to conduct this sitution normally: ignoring the new instance trigged, or to queue the instance until the trigger time meet the conditions, or direct error.

The following table shows the differences of the three kinds of threads in trigger time and dispatch time: If the system contains only the periodic threads, users can directly use the UCaS to analyze the schedulability, if the system contains aperiodic and sporadic threads, UCaS will remind users to set trigger time for them through the event producer.

UCaS provide the user with a friendly event production tool, its principle is show in figure 2. In this tool, aperiodic and sporadic threads contained in the AADL system instance are displayed in two lists. Users can choose one of these threads to set the trigger time for it. Of course, this is only a simulation of the situation, because usually, the aperiodic thread or the sporadic thread is difficult to be specific to a certain trigger point, but subject to some probability distribution. Because the time of scheduling process may be too long, so in the event producer, users do not need to set all the trigger point of each thread, but can specify the trigger period for the thread, and in the first period, set all the trigger point. Thus, in the consquent trigger period, the thread will be trigged just like the first period does.

For aperiodic thread, UCaS will find out that whether all the instances of aperiodic thread can be finished in the trigger period set by users, to ensure that the new instance of the next period will not be influented by the instance of this cycle. If not, UCaS will remind the user to change the trigger time of the thread.

For sporadic threads, UCaS has to ensure that in a single trigger period, the trigger points of threads are not too frequent. In other words, the interval of the trigger points between two isolated instances of threads is not too short. The value should not be less than its period. Otherwise, UCaS will remind the user to re-input the new trigger point.

After all the trigger periods and trigger points of aperiodic and sporadic threads are setted, UCaS sends all the information to the schedulability analysis procedure, and analyzed them together with the periodic threads.

div.head: C. Schdulability analysis
div.p: As for the real-time embedded systems, there are two scheduling algorithms mainly in use: RMS (Rate-Monotonic Scheduling) and EDF (Earliest Deadline First).

In AADL, thread is the basic execution unit of scheduling. A thread has some state: stop, sleep and active. A thread can wait for the dispatching, running, or block when access to the resources. Thread can also recover from an error, or in an unrecoverable error state. The properties of the thread can explain computing needs, the deadline and dispatching strategies.

The scheduling strategy set by user in AADL model can be extracted from the AAXL file which instantiate the system described in the AADL code. If the system contains only periodic threads, UCaS can use RMS or EDF algorithm to analyze the schedulability. But if there are aperiodic threads or sporadic threads, UCaS can only use EDF algorithm, it can not work with the RMS.

There are three clock variables in the scheduling module. One is the system clock ST, one is the running clock of thread named c , and one is the deadline clock t . ST is always plus 1, and will never be reset. Here c is instead of the actual range rate of the running clock, and t is instead of the range rate of the deadline clock. The various situations of clock and its range rate are shown in Figure 3.
At any time, if a thread has not yet completed its execution and its deadline has arrived, this system is not schedulable.
The scheduler must do the following things at each moment:
• Whether the currently running thread is completed.
If so, remove it.
• Whether there has a thread in the ready queue which its deadline has arrived and it has not completed its execution. If so, the system is not schedulable. • Whether there is new thread arrives.

• Adjust the priority of each thread in the ready queue dynamicly according to the scheduling strategy, choose the highest-priority thread to run, handle preemption. The time of schedulability analysis is computed as follow: get all the periods of preiodic, aperiodic and sporadic threads, compute the least common multiple, it is the time needed. If the system can run normally to the end of this time, and all threads are schedulable, then the system is schedulable. Because in the next scheduling cycle, the state of the entire system will be as same as it was in the last circle. Otherwise, the system is not schedulable, UCaS will stop analyzing and inform the user which thread has got to its deadline.

div.head: D. System simulator
div.p: This module gets the data from the scheduling procedure, and form an intuitive Gantt chart to show users that, how the state of the various threads in the system changes. Users can interact with UCaS through buttons: single step forward, single step backward, multi-step forward, multi-step backward, pause and resume.

Figure 5 is the interface of event producer. Figure 6 is a show of the running UCaS. The red block means the thread is running, while the blue one means the system is idle. The arrow upwards means the thread is ready to run, and the downwards one means the thread has completed its execution.

div.head: III. CONCLUSION
div.p: Real-time embedded systems have strict requirements about security, reliability and other non-functional properties. AADL is a kind of architecture analysis and design language to model the embedded system. It focuses on and tries to satisfy the non-functional properties of the embedded systems. The tool for schedulability analysis in this paper which called UCaS, combines the advantages of Furness and Times, can be easily used to analyze the embedded system described by AADL code, and simulate the whole exectuion process. From this simulation, users can know well about the system they construct, and adjust the attributes of threads to make the system schedulable.
The current UCaS can be improved as follow:

• Current UCaS considers only the case that all the threads are independent of each other, it dosen't consider the access to the sharing components, and this sitution will be added to the tool later. • In the design of UCaS, a thread's output event ports are not associated with another thread's dispatch port, but some times, the thread's output event ports may be related to another thread's dispatch port, in other words, the output event of one thread may result in dispaching of the another associated thread. The next version of UCaS will associate each thread with a behavior annex, which contains a state machine to explain the details of the communication between threads. • The time automation theory will be used in the schedulability analysis of AADL model. • According to the model-driven development process, AADL modeling, analysis, code generation, the three parts will be united in as a product line of embedded system.
